utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, could we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and Andres Vatter, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Rodney Dixon, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, Defence Counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. We have two witnesses scheduled for today. Let's hope that we'll be able to conclude their testimony today. Otherwise, the second witness will have to stay until next Monday. This is a possibility that I exclude a priori, but one never knows. When a party shows a document the witness, we have noticed that the other party tends to object if they do not see what the relation between the witness and the document is. If there is no link, in fact, that could be problematic. But the party that wants to proceed in this manner, they should at least show that there is an indirect link, if there isn't a direct one. And if so, they should ask the Trial Chamber to grant them leave to ask the question. Otherwise, we'll waste a lot of time. As you know, the Trial Chamber has always been fairly liberal and has -- when a question is put, we don't know what the purpose of the question might be. It might seem that the question doesn't make sense in relation to the document, but given the questions that follow, we might see the connection. This is why if an objection is made at the beginning of a question, we might later realise that the objection is groundless. But I would like to ask the parties to inform the Chamber of their intention to ask a question if the question is indirectly linked to a document. They should then explain why they want to ask the question. They should ask for leave, and we'll proceed in this manner. Otherwise, we'll waste a lot of time. I wanted to inform you of this to ensure that we can proceed as best as possible. With regard to Monday, the 15th of November, if the witnesses and the accused do not wish to be present here, then in such a case, it would be appropriate to say that there will no hearing on Monday, the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for what you have just informed us of. I would like to inform the Chamber that the Defence counsel has witnesses for Monday and for the other days of the week. But in accordance with the rights of the accused, we would like you to make the final decision as to whether we will be working on Monday. This will ensure that their rights are respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as I said, on Monday, the 16th -- correction, 15th of November, there won't be a hearing. There won't be a hearing on Monday, the 15th of November. Defence counsel may rest assured. Could the usher now call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Could you tell me whether you're receiving interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. Could the volume be put down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The usher will do that for you, the usher who is standing next to you. So before you testify here, and before you take the solemn declaration, could you please give me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Haris Jusic. I was born on the 24th of March 1958 in the village of Pode in Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work in the pension insurance company at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position, a military or civilian position? And if so, what kind of position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until the end of 1992, I was employed in a civilian company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in 1993, when I was no longer able to work, I became a member of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rank did you have? What were your duties? And which brigade were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I worked in the brigade. I was involved in legal matters. I was an officer in the security organ of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or a national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Before Defence commences its examination-in-chief, which will last for about an hour, I would like to provide you with some information. You have just taken the solemn declaration and said that you will speak the truth, which means that you shouldn't give false testimony which is punishable. Secondly, you should be aware that when answering questions, the information you provide cannot subsequently be used against you. The Rules grant you a form of immunity when testifying. The questions might appear complicated. If you don't understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. If the Judges before you don't have any written documents, we don't know who you are, what you may have done or what you may have seen. It is what you say when answering the questions that will inform us. That's why your questions are so important. In addition, you might be shown documents and asked about these documents by the parties examining you. So don't be surprised if you are asked to read a document and comment on it. The three Judges before you may at any point in time ask you questions, too. As a rule, the Judges prefer to wait for the parties to conclude their examination, but in certain circumstances we may intervene and ask you some questions. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. As we don't have much time today, since there is a second witness who will be following you, I will give the floor to the Defence Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the explanations provided to you by the President of the Trial Chamber, Mr. Jusic, I would like to ask you to make a break between my question and your answer. We both speak the same language, and my question needs to be translated for the Trial Chamber and all the others present in the courtroom. Are you clear on that?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you reside at the beginning of the war in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, I resided in the village of Pode, Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you worked in a civilian company. Can you please give us the name of that company and where was it based.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: It was the Sebesic timber company based in Travnik, and my workplace was in the sawmill in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, what are you by profession and where did you acquire your education?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in law, and I graduated from the school of law in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did you serve in the army? Which army did you serve in and if you did serve, what rank did you obtain?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, I served in the former Yugoslav People's Army. I was a foot soldier there. I did not have a rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the question put to you by the President of the Trial Chamber, you've told us that once you could no longer work you joined the ranks of the BiH Army, and that you became a member of the 306th Brigade. Tell me, please, what position did you hold? What tasks and duties did you have in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that my company was based in Nova Bila. Nova Bila is a Croatian village in the vicinity of Travnik. Since the relationships deteriorated towards the end of 1992 between Muslims and Croats, my then director told me that it would be best for me not to come for work because he could not guarantee my safety. I felt that myself, and I acted accordingly. I was sent home to wait. And since I resided in my village in 1992, I was in my native village. And as far as I know, the 306th Brigade was established towards the end of 1992. And obviously as a citizen, I was duty-bound to join that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, where was the command of your brigade? Where did you perform your duties as the official in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: The brigade command was in the administrative building of the coal mine in Bila. And up to the armed conflicts between the BiH Army and the HVO, every day I would go to work to that administrative building that belonged to the coal mine, save for the days on which I was sent somewhere else to perform tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your main tasks and duties as a legal officer in that security body?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Given my professional degree, I mostly performed the so-called administrative tasks. I would draft documents that were necessary. Those were purely legal tasks. I would be in charge of drafting some legal enactments, as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since your village -- no, let me rephrase that. What is the name of the general area in which your village, Pode, is situated? Or the place called coal mine where you performed your tasks?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: The entire area is known as the Bila region or the region of the Bila River. There is a little river there, its name is Bila. And that river gave the name to the entire area encompassing all the villages on both banks of that little river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, at the beginning of 1993 when you started performing your duties in the 306th Brigade, did you notice some foreigners from African and Asian countries appearing in the Bila region?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I told you that I could no longer work and I had to do something. It was my civic duty. And that's how I started working in my brigade. At that time, when I started working in my brigade, I didn't know anything about these people of Asian origin. However, I would come across them. I would see them from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know where these people came from? And since you saw them, can you tell the Trial Chamber what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about them. I did see them. They were a bit unusual. They had a different skin colour. Their skin was somewhat darker. They minded their own business. I did not come into any contact with them, either at that time or later, up to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the name that people started calling them at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The popular name that people gave them was the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are a lawyer, and as you've already told us, you were in charge of legal affairs. Before the war, did you know anything about who the mujahedin are and what is the meaning of that word?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: One might say that I didn't know anything about the mujahedin. I might have heard something on TV or on the TV news. I might have heard the name mentioned, but I didn't understand the concept.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you have never had any contacts with these people and you didn't know anything about them before that, did you ever at that time or later on think about the reason for which these foreigners might have arrived in the Bila region and in the area around Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a human being, I did think about that in the situation when the security deteriorated, and everybody had to look after themselves and their own life and safety. All of a sudden, people of a different skin colour came there, and I did not have a proper explanation for that, why this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any point in time, did you learn about the whereabouts of these people, where they were billeted?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I didn't know where they were billeted. I wasn't interested in that. However, as I was a member of the brigade throughout the entire 1993 up to the mid-1994, I did learn where they were located, where they were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where they stayed, where their camp was.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: In my area, in the Bila region, they were accommodated in Poljanice village in the abandoned Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up to June while performing your duties, did you ever go to the village of Mehurici? And if you did go there, where did you go? Did you ever visit the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Mehurici is not far from my village, the village where I was born. And it is not far from the place where the administrative building of the coal mine is. However, I didn't go to Mehurici, save for maybe on one or two occasions during the sixth time -- six-month period from the beginning of 1993 up to June 1993. I remember that I did go once. I didn't visit the school. I know that for a fact. On one occasion, I visited my colleague, the security officer of the 1st Battalion. He was accommodated in the house belonging to Ferid Jasarevic. This man had left the area in 1991 and moved to Austria together with his family. His house was therefore abandoned. It was rather big, and this is where the offices of my colleague from the 1st Battalion were. This building is at the very entrance to the village of Mehurici. I didn't go up to the school, but I know exactly where the school is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Jusic, did you know of any battalion of the 306th that was billeted in the school? If there was such a battalion, could you tell us which battalion it was.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I was not well informed of any of those things. However, I can Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond say that all of these buildings that were not privately owned, all the schools, and there were quite a few of them in the Bila region, were used either for the accommodation of refugees or for the accommodation of military formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were visiting your colleague, the security officer, in Mehurici or on any other occasion, did you learn whether members of the army or anybody else could freely enter the camp of the foreigners in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not discuss these people. At that time, they were not important. They were not a topic of our discussion. At that time, I did not even know exactly where they were located. This was prior to the conflict. So we did not discuss them. I don't even know whether at that time they were there or not. Maybe they were somewhere else, but I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1993, at the time when you joined the 306th Brigade, did you learn from any of the conversations in the command or other people that these foreigners were trying to get closer to the local population, or did you maybe learn about some problems involving these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I was never in any contact with these people. I was never close to them. However, in my conversations with my colleagues and other people, I did hear that these foreigners were trying to get closer to the local population, that they offered them certain things. I must say that the conditions that they offered them were much better than the ones that the army could provide for these people. Some locals finally did get in touch with them and cooperated with them, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, please tell me, in the area where your command was and where members of your brigade were, were there any other military formations there which did not belong to the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Up to the moment when the conflict broke out between the BiH Army and the HVO, in that area there were also members of the HVO. They were in their own villages, and the villages were either mixed - that is to say, the houses were mixed, they were close to each other - or they were in their own villages. Up to the moment when the conflict broke out, members of the HVO were in their houses. They moved about. I didn't know much about their movements. However, up to the moment the conflict broke out, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, Mr. Jusic, were there any incidents involving the BiH Army and the HVO in that area? What was the freedom of movement like? Did you witness any of those situations?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there were quite a number of incidents. Towards the end of 1992, I could no longer go to work, to the company that I used to work for. My director, who was a Croat, told me that my security was jeopardised, that my safety could not be guaranteed because the HVO had put up a check -- checkpoints on all the three exits from the Bila region. On the road towards Zenica, there was a checkpoint on Ovnak. It was manned by quite a few armed members of the HVO. At the beginning, these people just stood there. Then they started checking papers, and then finally they started prohibiting every movement. The same situation existed in Zabilje on the way to Vitez, and the same situation existed on the road to Travnik in Guca Gora. That means that the Muslim/Bosniak population was completely blocked. At the beginning, we could move around and travel, and after that, buses were forbidden passage. Private vehicles could still move about. And then on the eve of the conflict, nobody could exit the area. In addition to this region being blocked in that way, it was intersected by Croatian villages that we didn't dare go into unless we had to. If we could avoid entering Croatian villages, we did that rather than get involved in incidents. Before the conflict, people would get killed in their fields, on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jusic. I believe that you have described the situation pretty well. We've had other witnesses who have described the situation for us. I asked you whether you personally witnessed any ill treatment. Were you personally ill treated as a member of the command of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately this happened to me, too, in mid-May 1993. As I have already said, our command was in the administration building of the mine. Every evening we would return home, apart from those who couldn't do so because of their duties. A van transported us from the mine to Mehurici, brought us back in the evening. And in the morning, we would go to the command again in the same van. In mid-May 1993, on the 14th or 15th, as far as I can remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak up, Mr. Jusic, please.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: In mid-May 1993, on the 14th or 15th, I can't remember the exact date, we went off in the same van that we used to return to our homes with. And in the immediate vicinity of the command, the exit from a Croatian place called Baje, we were intercepted by a passenger vehicle, a private vehicle in which there were four HVO members who were fully armed. They forced us out of the van, and there was also a small TAM lorry which was privately owned. And the brigade members and the driver of that lorry were arrested, imprisoned at the same time. They forced us to lie down on our stomachs on the grass, and they cursed us and insulted us. They used the most insulting terms, the ugliest terms. And they took all our clothes, all the new clothes that we were wearing. They even took the shoes off one of our men. And the worst thing was that there was a man behind us who was cursing us, and he was pointing his rifle at us, which was loaded. This is what frightened us the most. The feeling I had at the time was terrible. Luckily, this did not last very long. It lasted as long as the four of them needed to take our things. As I said, to take all our clothes, which were new, to take the TAM lorry, and to take our van.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusic. Where were you on the 8th of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June 1993, I was in my village, in my house, in the house I was living in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that there were any large-scale armed conflicts in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: About a week before the armed clashes, I was sent to a forward command post on Vlasic. So for the last week, I was not in the Bila area because this position on Mount Vlasic is at least 20 kilometres away from the nearest village. When I returned, and this is why I was in my village, when I returned -- well, when one left the forward command post, one would go home and have a bit of a rest, have a bath and so on. That's why I was in the village then, and I had no duties at any time. I was practically on leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, did you ever leave the village after the 8th, and did anyone give you a task of any kind?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: A couple of days later, when the armed conflict calmed down and when I thought that I could go to the place where I was supposed to work safely, I then went to this workplace because in the meantime I had heard that the command was no longer in one place after the armed conflict had broken out. I found out that I was to go to Mehurici. I found out that there was work for me in Mehurici. So I reported to work in the village of Mehurici. I went to the school there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of task were you assigned at the time?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: My task was to take statements from the local people, imprisoned Croats who were accommodated in the Mehurici school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you, in fact, interview? Were there any criteria that were followed when interviewing people? Were you to interview everyone there, or was your task to interview certain people?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: My task was to take statements from the people who were there. They could have been military conscripts. The criteria that was to be followed was that we were to interview people who were between 20 and 60 years of age, the Croatian people who were there, women, children, and if there were any old people there were not interviewed by me [as Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many people did you take statements from when carrying out this task?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact number. But about 30 people, give or take a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you take these statements?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I did this in an office which was in the same school. And the people were kept in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you ask these people about?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked them about matters that might generally interest the military. I asked them whether they were HVO members; if they were, I asked them which brigade they had been in, who their commander was. If they knew, I would write this down, but on the whole they didn't know. I also asked them about the weapons they had, but I didn't obtain any important information about these things. But I obtained important information about whether they knew where mines had been laid and unexploded devices at positions around their villages. And on that occasion, we found out certain information. We removed a significant number of those mines and unexploded devices. I saw a small tractor. It was full of such devices. And that was the first time I saw explosives packed in a form that resembled salami.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, tell me whether you knew those people, or at least some of them, since they were neighbours of yours?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what hurt me the most. I knew most of those people. We had lived together, went to school together, used the same buses, worked in the same clinics, in the same factories. There had never been any problems among us. Now, all of a sudden, I was on one side; they were on another. This affected me as a man, but I performed my duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, tell me, how did you interview them? When interviewing these people, were they threatened or was force used? Or did you obtain the information you have just mentioned in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I can't say whether anyone used force when interviewing these people before I appeared. But when I interviewed these people, I did not use force. And as I have said, they were neighbours of mine with whom I had lived and with whom I had been on extremely good terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, you spoke to them and treated them as people you knew well. You treated them as your neighbours and friends. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, how long you were involved in these interviews; when did you finish with this work of yours?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps for five to seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that time anyone from the Red Cross came or anyone from international organisations? And were any objections raised about the way in which these people were treated?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any contact with such persons, but I do know that people from international humanitarian organisations came. And as far as I know, there were no objections concerning the accommodation and the conditions those people were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who took care of food and accommodation? Who took care of the security of those people while you were there?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: When I arrived there, security was provided by the civilian police, whereas food, as far as I know, was provided by the civilian protection. They ate the same food that we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the interviews that you conducted, did any of the people you interviewed complain about maltreatment, or were you able to observe traces of physical maltreatment on them?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such cases. None of them informed me of such cases. But believe me, I would have taken measures if I had had information about such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as far as you knew, did those people have adequate medical treatment? Were they provided with adequate medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as medical treatment is concerned, I think it was adequate. And quite by chance, their doctor was with them. If I'm not mistaken, her name was (redacted). She was with them in the immediate vicinity. She was given an office which was part of the hall they were kept in. I have been to that office. I've seen (redacted) there. I could see that she had medicine, medical supplies. I was present when she was giving them instructions of some kind. I think she was telling them to drink more liquid, et cetera. So I think that the medical treatment they were provided with was adequate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, when performing your duties did you ever find out why those people had been taken to that gym and why they were kept in the gym in the primary school?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I could mention two main reasons for which the people had been taken from their homes and placed in the gym. The first reason is that the HVO had attacked the Velika Bukovica village. That was before the 8th of June. It was on the 4th or 5th of June. And all the Muslim and Bosniak population from that village, 87 of them, were taken first to Nova Bila and then to Busovaca. And they were taken away as prisoners. So that's the first reason for which people of Croatian nationality were gathered in one place. The main reason was to proceed with an exchange when the conditions were right. The second reason, which for me is more important than the first one, the second reason is that if people had remained in their houses, in such a case, there could have been incidents of various kinds. People could have been killed by various individuals for various reasons. And also because of the presence of the mujahedin themselves, who were in such a state at the time that even we, the local population, were a little frightened of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have now mentioned the reasons. But I would like to know where you went after you had finished interviewing those 30 people. Were you assigned any other tasks?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: When this job was completed, I was sent to join the main body of the command which was in Krpeljici. I would call it a main body of the command because up there, I found the commander. This is where I was sent to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell me whether you took any statements from anybody up there and who these people were.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were Croats up there as well. They were also accommodated in two different places. There was a building which we called the youth centre, and this is where they were accommodated, but not as many of them as in Mehurici. And there was also another house where they were because they could not all fit in one building. This second house was of a smaller size. So these people were accommodated in a Croatian house. I can't remember who the owner of that house was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, did there come a time when you started taking statements from Bosniaks as well? And when you started doing that, were statements taken under the same conditions, or did you treat people differently?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I was taking statements from ones and the others, and therefore I can confirm this and say that I took statements from Bosniaks whose families had been taken to Busovaca. When the exchange finally took place, I took statements from those who returned from those places where the HVO had kept them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, did you personally ever get involved in the -- in any of the exchanges? Were you ever consulted on any of the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I was never involved in an exchange. I never had any contacts from anybody from the international organisations regarding exchanges. I didn't have contacts with people from the international organisation on any of the issues. I was an official in the brigade, and I did what my superiors told me to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You continued working in the 306th in the security body, and according to some information, after the combat operations, there was Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond plundering and burning buildings in the general area. Did you have any information about these incidents? Do you know who the perpetrators were? Did you in the security body undertake any measures against the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there were such situations, and there was plunder. Houses were set on fire. We did take measures against members of our own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What measures were those?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: The commander would order people to be remanded in custody. When we discovered perpetrators, we would take statements and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you are a lawyer by profession, before you did these things, were you ever involved in criminal investigation or any similar thing?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: No. I was never involved in any military or police business or law enforcement business. When I joined the army, I was given this job because of my degree, because of my profession. I don't know whether I was successful or not, but I do think that I did well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the witness to be shown a few documents. I would kindly ask Madam Usher to give the documents to the witness, and this would bring my examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, can you please look at this document bearing number 1444. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it signed by?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I'm the one who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this one of the documents that testify to the fact that you remanded in custody members of your brigade for whom it had been established that they were involved in theft?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following document, 1448. Is this also one of your documents that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this one of the ways in which you dealt with the perpetrators of criminal acts? Is this how you informed the competent prosecutor's office of the crime?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. First, the military police would carry out investigation, collect information, and then they would inform me. I would process this information. And whenever there were elements for criminal report, I would draft a criminal report. The person would be remanded in custody. This was a situation in which people from Krpeljici had to be escorted to Travnik. It would not be usual for me to sign this. It would be my commander or assistant commander who signed such documents. However, if they were not present and something had to be done, I was the one who signed these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, you said you have a degree in law, and you were in charge of legal affairs. Was there anybody else in your legal body who had any legal knowledge or knowledge of the police work, the security work?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I can say that none of us had the necessary knowledge and experience to perform these duties. As far as I know, in the body that I worked in, nobody had that experience. Only one person had been a member of the military police as far as I remember. The rest of us were amateurs, laymen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the brigade or in the army, was there any training of soldiers and officers? Were you aware of any training organised for soldiers and officers?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of some training because people became members of the brigade and its bodies without ever having dreamt of having to do that. However, the situation was as it was. We had to do things, and I know that measures were being taken by the superior commands to organise courses and training in order to teach people how to perform duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Document 1455. That's document number 3. Can you please look at it and tell me whether this was one of the ways of organising education for the staff members ranging from company further up.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you discovered perpetrators, you would take disciplinary measures or you would file a criminal report. Did you have any difficulties when you wanted to find out who the perpetrators were, and what was the cause of those difficulties?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: We met with all sorts of difficulties. Nothing was simple in our work. From the simplest things -- for example, there was no paper, there was nothing to write on or with. We didn't have petrol, so we could not drive to the place where the crime was committed. We didn't have personnel that would provide security if that was necessary. We met with all sorts of problems. And in such an impossible situation, we did to the best of our abilities in order to prevent all sorts of crime. The situation was impossible; however, we worked to the best of our abilities in order to elucidate crimes, discover perpetrators, and punish them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there cases of impersonation or groups appearing without any documents whose identity could not be established? If there were such cases, did you take any measures against those people?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: There were all sorts of cases. Our mission was impossible. For example, after having performed their shifts, people did not go back to the barracks. They went back to their homes. So they would spend some time on the lines performing military duties and after their shift, they would be free for up to seven days. For example, they would spend seven days on the line and seven days at home on leave. And during those periods where they were on leave, these people would move about. They would do all sorts of things. We tried to prevent that as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Document Number 1456. This is a document sent by the 3rd Corps to the assistants for security of all the brigade. Since you were a member of the security of your brigade, were you aware of these measures that were suggested or ordered by this document of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I am aware of these cases, and such cases. That's why the document of this nature was sent, in order to prevent such cases. For example, a person is a member of a unit and gets this unit's ID number. And then for various reasons - for example, their families would want to move - we had a lot of refugees and displaced persons who moved quite a lot within the territory of one municipality or several municipalities. For example, we had people from Karaula. It's a village in Travnik Municipality. They settled in the Bila region. They were members of the 306th Brigade, and then they left. But they continued wearing the uniform and the ID card of their former brigade, the 312th Brigade. And this brought all sorts of different situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, could you please look at Document Number 5 and tell me whether you are familiar with this document, first of all.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I've already said something about the contents of this document. This document was drafted at the moment when civilians, women, children, and elderly from Velika Bukovica, a village which was the first one to be attacked in the Bila region, returned from the detention in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document speaks to treatment they were exposed to. People whom you interviewed in Mehurici school, did they ever tell you about being treated by BiH Army members in an appropriate way [sic]?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: These people never told me that. And I wish to claim that they were never treated in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Jusic, you've told us that it was the military police that provided security for these people in the Mehurici school. You were a member of the 306th Brigade. Can you tell me something about the authorities? Were you authorised and have control over the army, the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond military police, or civilian police?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the measures that we took? The civilian police was authorised to have control over the civilians, and we were authorised to have control only over the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were ever the mujahedin under the control of the 306th Brigade? Did you ever any authority over them?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I said that I never had contact of any kind with the mujahedin. And if they had been members of our brigade, I would have had contact with them. Without doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake in the translation of my question. It's page 25, line 18. I said at the end "Mr. Jusic," -- I said "finally, Mr. Jusic, you said that the civilian police provided security," whereas it says "the military police provided security" in the transcript. So could this be corrected, please. Thank you, Mr. Jusic, I have no more questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We only have a few questions for Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jusic, you were born in the village of Pode in the Bila Valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the village of Pode, whereas Podovi is a Croatian village in vicinity. It in fact is the same thing. My village is officially called Pode, but some maps in land registries it's referred to as Podovi, but in fact the village is Pode.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, you were a member of the 306th Brigade and you worked in that brigade as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As a lawyer, a member of the 306th Brigade, since you spent 1993 in that area, I assume that you know whether there were any other BH Army units that had been organised in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the 306th Brigade, there were -- or rather, there was another brigade, the 314th Brigade. And I have said that there were also HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I say that in 1993, especially in the spring and summer of 1993, in the region of Mehurici and in the region of the other villages and in the Bila Valley, there were no units and no 7th Brigade Battalion, you would agree with me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the 7th Muslim Brigade was never in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another 10 minutes before the break. I'll give the floor to the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jusic. My name is Mathias Neuner, and I am representing the Prosecution here. I will put a few questions to you now, and then we will have a break in a few minutes. Your Honour, I will propose I put a few questions about the documents now, and then take an early break. This will take only 2 or 3 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look, please, at Document Number 1, again, Mr. Jusic, and look under the heading "Reason." Is it fair to say that this decision which you have in front of you relates to crime committed against the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you turn now to please Document Number 2 in front of you. Please look at page 1, number 6. And there it states, inter alia, "all members of the 1st Battalion of the 325 Mountain Brigade." So the perpetrators, and that's a question actually, the perpetrators were all ABiH members?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I have another question for you: If you please look in this document now under the heading "Statement of Reasons." Do you find this?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did the perpetrators use a van belonging to the ABiH to commit their crime?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here, that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the crime itself, was it committed in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the date of the crime, this was September 1993; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me find the date. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I would ask to go for an early break, and I would continue with my questioning thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now 10.26. We'll resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, I want to continue where I just left you before the break. I showed you a document about Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And with the leave of the Chamber I would like to show the Document P204 to the witness. This document is also relating to Guca Gora. And on the addressee list under number 4, it's addressed to the military police of the 306th. That's why I'm showing it to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at the first paragraph, Mr. Jusic, it talks about torching, and it talks about mass plunder, is it?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Should I have a look at it? Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Read it just -- just read the first paragraph above "Order" please, for yourself, and if you could please briefly confirm that it relates to torching and mass plunder. Just the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this section does refer to torching and mass plunder. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the same sentence, it talks also about the perpetrators, the perpetrators being members of the civilian population and individual members of the BH Army. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the document is stamped from the 18th of June. You can see this on top. So some measures have been ordered on the 18th of June. Since the area was taken over on the 8th of June already, why, if I may ask you, and you were testifying on direct about this, why were measures only taken on the 18th? Why not earlier?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what my opinion is. Measures were taken before the 18th of June as well, but combat activity didn't cease on the 18th of June. Combat activities continued. The military police was engaged in the course of combat on the whole in order to engage in military action. But it wouldn't be true to say that they only started taking measures on the 18th of June. Measures were taken before, to the extent that this was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. Was there a curfew imposed earlier? As you said, measures were taken earlier. Was there a curfew imposed in order to stop people going out and taking goods from others?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that there was a curfew. But in a certain sense, there was one because that was a combat zone, and it was very dangerous to move around in the evening. From dusk to dawn, it was extremely dangerous to move around. Whoever did so did so at his or her own risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just if you say yes or no: To your knowledge, was there an order imposing a curfew in Guca Gora area given after the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I can neither confirm nor deny that, but I would sooner say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to talk a little bit about your background.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And can I please ask the usher to show the witness a document, a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at the B/C/S version -- look at page 1, please, in Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the upper left-hand corner, it dates from February 1993, the document. And if you look at the very, very end of the document, the last page, please, for a second, it is signed by an officer for security affairs. Can you please confirm this.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I haven't read the document, but on the basis of what I can see at the beginning and the end, I would say that this is the first time I've seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look to page 6, please, of this document - I can show you in a second why I'm showing you this document - under the heading "306 Brigade," please. You'll find your name there and your position.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you read the relevant section mentioning your name and then onwards.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, read it out aloud? Should I read it to myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just read your name out loud, and the sentence following.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: "Jusic, Haris, the 24th of April 1998 [as interpreted], graduated lawyer, an officer for legal matters will be engaged according to need."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, 24th of March 1958 was the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It says you were a security affairs officer and employed when there was a need. Can you just explain what that means. You were employed full time or you were employed less than full time? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I think that there is a mistake here. While I was working, I said worked until the end of 1992 in my company. And I was then engaged according to need. And from the beginning of 1993, I started working full time, so to speak, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying this. Who was your superior when you worked full time?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the assistant commander for security was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you state his name, please, for the record. 7 A.Well, I can say what his name was, as it states here, Delalic, Asim, son of 8 Ramo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many staff in the military security department were employed at the time, spring, summer 1993? Just give a number. Just mention a number, please. 12 A. You're referring to the department I was in, and just to that department?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: There were three, or rather four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Four persons. And in Mehurici, how many people were employed in the military security organ in Mehurici, spring -- April to June, let's say, 1993? Just give a number. In the 306 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was one person in each battalion. We would call such persons security persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was his name? The 1st Battalion of the 306 in Mehurici, what was the name of the person, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I find it difficult to remember names, but I think his name was Hasan Zukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Document P661. And for the Judges, for Your Honours, I wish to show this document because the witness has testified on direct about the presence of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And this document relates to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The document dates from 6 April. And if you look at the second paragraph, please. Does it mention the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Could you give me time to read the paragraph. This paragraph refers to individual members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I said that the 7th Muslim Brigade wasn't present in this area, but there were individuals who were born in that area. They had their houses there. They lived there, and they were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. And naturally, they would occasionally go home. And this is how it was. That's my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions about Miletici, the Miletici incident in April 1993. You said you were -- first of all, were you involved in any direct way in the investigations relating to the Miletici incident?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I know very little about this incident. I did not participate in that event in any way. I didn't participate in anything leading up to it. I didn't participate in it or anything that happened after it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sir, I was just whether you participated in a direct way in an investigation occurring thereafter. Did you?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said there were three other colleagues in the military security department in the command, and one colleague in the military security department in Mehurici. Did they participate in any investigation?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is it fair to summarise, then, that none of these four persons participated in any investigation after the Miletici incident?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: According to my information, that would be the case. I am referring to the security department of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You're not referring to the 1st Battalion security department? You don't know about the 1st Battalion security department?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. However, I assume if there had been an investigation of any sort, I would have been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move on to the incidents in the school of Mehurici. You testified about this. To your knowledge -- first of all, you were called by somebody to report to the school in order to do interrogations. Who was telling you to come to the school and do some interrogations?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: It was my obligation to report to the command because that's where I worked. I inquired as to where I was supposed to go and work because the command was split into three different places. I was told to go to Mehurici, and it was my superior, the assistant commander for security, who told me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And arriving in Mehurici, to whom did you speak first?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember that. When I approached the school, there were a lot of people there. I entered the school. I met with my superiors, and then my superior told me to take statements from these people. At that moment, I didn't know how many people there were, what this was all about. He told me which people to take statements from. He told me, "this is going to be your office, and this is where you are going to work. We will organise for people to be brought to you one by one. As soon as one statement is taken, the next person will be shown in." And this is how I proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the superior to whom you spoke first, was he the assistant commander for security in the 306? Your superior from Bila?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, I can't state that he was the first I spoke to. There were other people there. I may have talked to somebody else before him. When it came to my work, I first spoke to him, to my superior from the admin building of the coal mine in Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How long did your superior -- let me rephrase that, please. On what day exactly did you arrive in Mehurici in June?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. It was after the 8th of June, maybe three to four days after that date. But I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And your superior, did he mention in the conversation you had with him that he was arriving shortly before you or he was there already for days?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that. I wouldn't be able to give you a precise answer to that question. After the conflict, the command was scattered, ended up in three different places. At the moment of the conflict, whether he was in Rudnik or in Mehurici, I really wouldn't know. But those who had been in Krpeljici, they travelled from Travnik, and they just could not go any further. And that's why they stayed put in Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: When you first spoke to your superior, you had the impression that your superior was informed about what has happened earlier? I'm referring to the -- why were people there and that people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Nobody was killed. Can you please clarify. Which killed people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is on their feet. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness has already intervened, the Prosecutor's question referred to something that the witness has never said as having seen or heard or witnessed. The witness himself intervened, so there's no need for my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I apologise, Witness. There were many people in the school, you testified.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you know the reason why these people were in the school?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered my question. According to him, there were two reasons, and I don't see the need to repeat the same answers again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind repeating the reasons for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question to be more precise. Had your superior -- I'm talking now only about the persons, the Croat persons who had been killed in the Maline-Bikose incident, no longer to the persons in the school. Had your superior, by the time you spoke to him, heard about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President -- Mr. President, my objection stands. My learned friend should maybe first ask the witness whether he has ever heard about this, and only then whether his superior had ever heard of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are faced with a difficulty here. Can you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Have you - I rephrase the question - ever heard that Croats on the 8th of June had been killed by - I phrase it very abstractly - Muslim forces? I don't want to indicate any unit or whatever. Have you heard that 30 to 35 Croats had been killed on the 8th of June? In Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my learned friend be more precise in his question. Such a wide-scoped name, "Muslim forces," doesn't mean anything. It can mean anything, the mujahedin, the army from Herzegovina, certain members of the BiH Army, and so on and so forth. So the question put in this way is absolutely vague. It's not precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the question does require a reply. I'm going to ask the questions. Witness, I'm going to raise this issue. When you met with your superior who would give you the task of take statements from the people who were accommodated in the school, at the moment when you met with him, did you discuss with him the totality of the events that had taken place in the area? Or did you only discuss the testimonies and statements of these particular individuals? Can you please answer my question. What was it all about? My question is rather widely put, so it gives you the freedom to say whatever. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the school in Mehurici and when I met with my superior, the only thing he told me was to take statements from the people that would be brought to me by policemen, one at a time. We did not engage in any other conversation. After that, he went somewhere. I don't know where. I suppose, since the command was in a different place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Your superior did not mention in this conversation with you what might have happened in Miletici or in Maline. He never touched that topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If after such a question, the witness has said "yes," but the witness said "no." The only topic that they discussed were the statements of the people in the school. This was just a comment for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did any of the 30 witnesses you interviewed talk about the fact that at some point in time, people were separated from their column and walked back? Or did they not mention anything at all in this regard on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: At that moment, people answered my questions, and the answers were recorded word for word. Nobody said anything to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My last question relating to the killed Croats would be: Were you aware about any investigation conducted at the time when you were doing interviews? I mean by your colleagues who were there also. Did you learn anything about investigative activity into such events?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the information that I got from the people who were brought there, or are you speaking in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I am speaking in general terms. You told me already the witnesses didn't say anything. Your superior didn't say anything. But maybe some of your colleagues who were on the spot as well, they were engaged in some kind of investigation, and they might have mentioned something.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, nobody mentioned anything to me. After a certain time, I did hear about those questions. However, during the period while I was taking the statements, I didn't know a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will come in a second to who told you later. Just for the record, so neither a member of the military security service you met there in Mehurici after 8th of June nor a member of the military police or a member of the civilian police ever mentioned any investigation going on in relation to the killed Croats near Maline-Bikose.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I was not aware of anything at that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But you said later you learned about this. When was the first time you learned about this and from whom, please?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: It was maybe a month or so later. As to the person I heard it from, I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Was this a work-related conversation where you learned about the killing of the Croats, or was it just a private conversation?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: It must have been a private, informal conversation. It was not work related.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sir, would it be fair to say that the killing of Croats wasn't discussed in the month following this incident? The killing of the Croats wasn't discussed at work at all?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer either by saying yes or by saying no. I said that I had performed tasks given to me by my superior. I don't know whether he or other people knew about it. I didn't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move to the questioning of detainees in the Mehurici school. First of all, you testified that none of us or your colleagues had any necessary knowledge before you came on the job. You came basically -- let me rephrase that. You testified on page 22, page 23 that none of your colleagues had the necessary knowledge. Starting from there, you mentioned only one military police officer had knowledge. What type of knowledge were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: There were no educated officers, as far as I know. And as for the knowledge that you're inquiring about, I believe that one had been a military policeman in the former JNA, and this is the type of knowledge I Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did this military policeman transfer his knowledge to you or to your other colleagues? Was there a kind of transfer of knowledge so that you were in a position to do examinations?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not even sure that he was a military policeman. I just assumed that he was. And I'm referring to our assistant commander for security. And obviously, whatever he knew, whatever he could convey to us in terms of knowledge he did, as much as he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you also testified about training you received, I assume, in international humanitarian law. So you would consider yourself being qualified to do such interrogations with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: I did not have any trainings save for what I did at the university in law school. However, when I was a student, I didn't even dream of having to take part in the war. When I did that part of my education, I just did it so as to be able to pass the exam. I didn't do it really seriously, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sir, if a prisoner of war would sit in front of you in the Mehurici school, you testified you were talking to 30 persons --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness never mentioned that those were prisoners of war. He testified that he was supposed to take statements from the able-bodied men who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the Prosecution has put to the witness that he has a degree in law, and that during his education he was educated on international law. The witness replied that when they did that during the war, it was a different thing. From that, the Prosecution - please look at line 10 - has put to the witness as follows. They were going to ask him a legal question. He has a degree in law, and they were going to ask him a question of a legal nature. And by the answer, they could test the credibility of the witness because the witness was in charge of all the legal and security affairs in the 306th Brigade. It should be noted that in the document that you yourself drafted, you even took a decision to detain somebody. And this was signed by yourself, sir. So the Chamber will allow the question of legal nature that the Prosecution was going to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: If you're waiting for my answer, then I'd be grateful it you could repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you testified 30 persons were coming or were interviewed by you in the Mehurici school, before you started that interview, what would be the first information you put to this witness or to this person?

utterances.speaker: HARIS JUSIC
utterances.text: If such a person came to my office, I would naturally tell the person to sit down, and I would then ask the person to give me his or her particulars. I did this in case information was obtained via a criminal report. This is why I took down the individual's particulars. Then I asked the person some questions about what I already mentioned. We were interested in what these people knew about HVO units, about weapons, about mines and explosive devices. These are the sorts of questions that I asked such individuals. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sir, wouldn't there be first a right of this prisoner of war? Wouldn't you need to inform the person that he has a right as a prisoner of war? Wouldn't that be the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is proceeding a little too rapidly, perhaps. I'll put the question to you. You carry out an investigation. You have someone before you who you want to question. You're a legal officer. When you have someone before you, the person has a certain status. Today, your status is that of a witness. The individuals you had before you, what was their legal status? What was the legal status of the individuals who were questioned? These individuals apparently weren't free to leave as they pleased because you yourself said that a civilian police platoon guarded the facilities. Could you tell us what the status of the people you questioned was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these people had the same status as the civilians who were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that these people had the status of the people who were accommodated there. If I have understood you correctly, the Mehurici school was something like a big hotel. They had been provided with accommodation there. But when you're staying in a hotel, no one comes to ask you very precise questions about how you lived, about who you had to report to, et cetera. The questions that you asked these people, were these questions that corresponded to the status of a woman, for example, who had a baby in her arms? Were they questions that might be put to such a woman? How would you define this status? This is what we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have already said that people had been provided with the best conditions we could provide them with. They had the same sort of accommodation as the Muslims, the Bosniaks, in the school in Han Bila. These were Muslims that had been expelled from areas that were taken over by Serbs. So they had the same sort of accommodation in the school in Mehurici as the Bosniaks did in the school in Han Bila. We couldn't provide them with better accommodation. I said that we took statements from individuals who were there and who were between 20 and 60 years of age. We believed that they might be HVO members. This is why we took statements from them. As for women, children, and the elderly, we didn't take any statements from them. They were not questioned. No statements were taken from these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a person before you said, "Sir, thank you for asking me these questions, but I'm going to leave now. I'm going home," would it have been possible for this person to leave the premises? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was war. You know that in wartime, people have a certain status. There are members of the military and there are civilians. There is a law that is applied in times of war. So my question is as follows: You're a legal officer, and in the 306th Brigade, you're responsible for these legal matters. What was the applicable law with regard to the people who were in this school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The laws in force were the laws that had been passed by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, the laws in force were the laws that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had adopted. And I'm speaking as a lawyer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But according to the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, civilians have the right to move around freely. They can only be arrested if there is an investigation of a judicial kind, and when they are guarded, as far as I can remember, they can only be guarded for a three-day period. A judge has to authorise detention for a period exceeding three days. That's usually the applicable law. So I don't know how you interpret the law. But the Prosecution has asked you a question, and the Judges are asking you this question, too. The people kept in the school, what rights did they have? What duties did they have? And what was it possible for them to leave the premises? On a number of occasions, you said that you had provided them with accommodation and that you provided them with food.
